INTRODUCTION
Below, the Alaska Supreme Court accepted that “the
‘touchstone’ of the excessiveness inquiry is proportionality.” At the same time, however, the court developed a
standard that writes the “gravity of the defendant’s offense” (United States v. Bajakajian, 524 U.S. 321, 337
(1998)) out of the analysis. That error warrants reversal.
The State devotes much of its response to a theory the
decision below did not adopt and that contradicts the
State’s own cert-stage framing of the question presented.
The State’s top-line argument now is that the Excessive
Fines Clause imposes no proportionality check at all on
any forfeiture of property used in an offense. But the
Court rejected that workaround decades ago. “[T]he test
for the excessiveness of a punitive forfeiture,” the Court
has held, “involves solely a proportionality determination.” Id. at 333-34. And analogies to historical in rem “instrumentality” forfeitures—the keystone of the State’s
argument here—are “inapposite” and “irrelevant” and
“indicate nothing about the proportionality” of modern
punitive ones. Id. at 330, 333, 340-41. As for the federal
government’s submission, every one of its examples of extreme eighteenth-century forfeitures culminated in the
government’s dropping the case and returning the vessel.
On the question presented, the State has less to say.
It concedes (Br. 27) that “[a]n Excessive Fines Clause
analysis requires an examination of a defendant’s culpability.” But it maintains (Br. 41-42) that courts cannot conduct that examination when a fine is set by statute; if a
defendant falls within the class lawmakers meant to “target,” that ends the analysis. That view captures the
Alaska Supreme Court’s error perfectly. Under any statute, every convicted defendant will be “within the class of
persons targeted by the statute.” Pet. App. 20a. Indeed,

2


the decision below could not have been clearer: However
minor the misconduct, what matters is the harm “addressed in the legislative history.” Pet. App. 25a n.94. Under the standard below, the gravity of the offense is the
same whether you’re dealing kilos of cocaine or giving
your spouse an Ambien. Or, in Alaska, whether your offense involves sixty pallets of whisky or a six-pack of Budweiser. So long as the legislature “reasonably” thought its
statute addressed a serious problem (Resp. Br. 39), the
defendant’s particular wrongdoing is irrelevant.
The State’s arguments spotlight that standard’s flaws.
According to the State, what the Excessive Fines Clause
demands is not that courts evaluate the defendant’s offense based on “the facts of [the] particular case,” Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 337 n.10, but that judges somehow
divine what subclass of defendants lawmakers subjectively wanted to target—then defer. Resp. Br. 34. How
that standard is supposed to work is anyone’s guess; how
it can be squared with the notion of a Bill of Rights is similarly unanswerable. The correct approach is the simpler
one: Facts matter, and a court evaluating “the gravity of
the defendant’s offense” must consider, not just the offense in the abstract, but the defendant’s own misconduct.
ARGUMENT
I. The State’s bid to exempt its forfeiture from any
proportionality standard lacks merit.
The State leads with a theory the Alaska Supreme
Court did not adopt. Where that court acknowledged (correctly) that “the ‘touchstone’ of the excessiveness inquiry
is proportionality,” Pet. App. 16a, the State now advances
a different position: Across the board, legislatures may
impose “mandatory forfeiture of the instruments of
crimes without running afoul of the Excessive Fines
Clause”—proportionality be damned. Resp. Br. 18; U.S.

3


Br. 13 (“Forfeiture of an instrumentality of a crime does
not depend on an assessment of the value of the property
or the relation between that value and the offender’s conduct.”). Because Jouppi’s airplane was linked to an offense (so the argument goes), its forfeiture necessarily
comports with the Excessive Fines Clause—however minor the offense, however great the forfeiture.
First off: The Court need not entertain this theory unless it’s so inclined. At the certiorari stage, the State’s own
framing of the question presented acknowledged that “[a]
forfeiture violates the Excessive Fines Clause if it is
‘grossly disproportional to the gravity of a defendant’s offense.’” Br. in Opp. i. The airplane’s use in an offense was
merely “[a]n additional factor” in the analysis (Br. in Opp.
29)—not, as the State says now, the entire analysis. Below, moreover, the State’s argument differed again: It
maintained that Jouppi’s forfeiture “falls outside the
Eighth Amendment” altogether. State’s Alaska Sup. Ct.
Br. 24. But see Br. in Opp. 31 (“The forfeiture at issue is
subject to the Eighth Amendment[.]”). Square corners, it
seems, are for pilots, not prosecutors.
Rule 15.2 aside, the State’s theory is foreclosed by
precedent, unsupported by history, and unworkable in
practice.
A. For modern punitive forfeitures, the Court has
rejected as “irrelevant” analogies to historical
in rem forfeitures.
1.  Bajakajian forecloses the State’s theory. There,
much like here, the federal government pursued a criminal in personam forfeiture, 524 U.S. at 328; invoked “historic forfeitures of property tainted by crime,” id. at 329;
and argued that, for “instrumentalities of crime,” the Excessive Fines Clause requires no “additional inquiry into
the culpability of the owner or the property’s economic

4


value.” U.S. Br. at 11, United States v. Bajakajian, 524
U.S. 321 (1998) (No. 96-1487). The Court rejected that argument root and branch. Historical in rem forfeitures
rested on “the fiction that the action was directed against
‘guilty property,’” not “the offender himself.” 524 U.S. at
330. Sound or not, the Court reasoned, that fiction meant
those forfeitures “were viewed as nonpunitive” and thus
“outside the domain of the Excessive Fines Clause.” Id.
at 331. Criminal in personam forfeitures, meanwhile, descend from “a different historical tradition”: They “have
historically been treated as punitive” and are a relative
novelty in our legal system. Id. at 332 & n.7.1
Given that disconnect, the government’s “instrumentality” analogy missed the mark. “Instrumentalities,” the
Court explained, is shorthand for the “‘guilty property’”
historically “forfeited in civil in rem proceedings.” Id. at
333. But when the government seeks “to punish” someone—by, for example, “proceeding against him criminally”—any guilty-property fiction collapses; the forfeiture is “clearly punishment” targeting a person. Id. at 333,
344. It is thus “irrelevant” whether the property can be
termed “an instrumentality.” Id. at 333. “[T]he forfeiture
is punitive” regardless, and “the test for the excessiveness
of a punitive forfeiture involves solely a proportionality
determination.” Id. at 333-34.
2.  The State’s efforts to circumvent Bajakajian’s reasoning fail. At the certiorari stage, the State admitted

1 Speaking only through a one-judge opinion from Alaska’s intermediate court, the State suggests (Br. 3-5) that in personam forfeitures
were as common in Alaska as in rem forfeitures. That is incorrect:
Much like the early statutes discussed in Bajakajian, the cited nineteenth-century statutes were understood as authorizing in rem forfeitures. See, e.g. , The Louisa Simpson , 1 Alaska Fed. 50 (D. Or.
1871).

5


that Bajakajian held “irrelevant whether the currency
was an ‘instrumentality’” because the forfeiture was in
personam. Br. in Opp. 3-4. Today? Crickets. Its only attempt to distinguish Bajakajian is to assert that the “history of forfeiture of vessels is distinct from forfeitures of
currency.” Resp. Br. 22. But the line that matters is between punitive forfeitures and non-punitive ones, not between dollar bills and sailing ships. Every time in rem
forfeitures were raised in Bajakajian—goods (Harford),
ships ( The Palmyra ), automobiles ( Van Oster ), land
(Dobbins’s Distillery )—the Court set them aside. Because “they were not considered . . . punishment for an offense,” the Court reasoned, they “indicat[ed] nothing
about the proportionality of the punitive forfeiture at issue here.” 524 U.S. at 340-41 (citing id. at 330-32, discussing ships, cars, and land). Contra U.S. Br. 21.
The federal government fares no better. It notes that
Bajakajian’s cash would not have qualified as an instrumentality in any event. U.S. Br. 18. But either way, the
Court was clear: When a forfeiture is punitive it is “irrelevant whether [the property] is an instrumentality.” 524
U.S. at 333.  The federal government also notes (Br. 19-
20) that Bajakajian characterized certain early monetary penalties as non-punitive too, citing their “remedial
purpose of reimbursing the Government.” 524 U.S. at 342.
But that a second analogy failed does not muddy the
Court’s twice-stated rejection of the government’s reliance on early in rem forfeitures.
3.  Lower courts have taken this Court at its word, another point the State leaves unmentioned. Every court of
appeals and state high court to consider the issue applies

6


a proportionality standard to punitive forfeitures—including of property connected to a crime.2
Against all this, the State invokes (Br. 22-24, 39-40)
Justice Scalia’s suggestion that, for in rem forfeitures,
the excessive-fines standard might look simply to “what
property has been ‘tainted’ by unlawful use.” Austin v.
United States, 509 U.S. 602, 627 (1993) (opinion concurring in part and concurring in the judgment). Left unmentioned: that even under Justice Scalia’s view, the standard
would likely be “different” for “in personam forfeitures.”
Id. For “monetary fine[s],” he remarked, “the touchstone
is value of the fine in relation to the offense”—and precedent “indicate[s] that the same is true for in personam
forfeiture.” Id. (citing Alexander v. United States , 509
U.S. 544, 558 (1993)). Unsurprisingly, neither the State
nor the federal government identifies any decision adopting their proportionality-free standard. Elsewhere, in
fact, the Solicitor General has freely acknowledged Bajakajian’s import: Even for property involved in a crime,
the Excessive Fines Clause measures “the magnitude of
the forfeiture” against “the gravity of the defendant’s
crime,” including “the culpability of the particular defend-

2 E.g., United States v. 45 Claremont St., 395 F.3d 1, 6 (1st Cir. 2004);
von Hofe v. United States, 492 F.3d 175, 184 (2d Cir. 2007); Yskamp
v. DEA, 163 F.3d 767, 773 (3d Cir. 1998); United States v. Ahmad,
213 F.3d 805, 815 n.4 (4th Cir. 2000); United States v. 415 E. Mitchell
Ave., 149 F.3d 472, 477-78 (6th Cir. 1998); United States  v. Dodge
Caravan, 387 F.3d 758, 762-63 (8th Cir. 2004); United States  v.
Ferro, 681 F.3d 1105, 1115 (9th Cir. 2012); United States v. Wagoner
Cnty. Real Est. , 278 F.3d 1091, 1100-01 nn.7-8 (10th Cir. 2002);
United States v. 817 N.E. 29th Dr., 175 F.3d 1304, 1309-10 (11th Cir.
1999); 15th Cir. Drug Enf’t Unit ex rel. Richardson v. $20,771, 878
S.E.2d 868, 877-78 (S.C. 2022); State v. Timbs, 134 N.E.3d 12, 26 (Ind.
2019).

7


ant.” Br. in Opp. at 7, Cheeseman v. United States, 562
U.S. 1060 (No. 09-1470).
B. History reinforces the Court’s reasoning.
1.  The State and the federal government observe that
historical statutes authorized in rem forfeitures of vessels and call it “willfully blind” to apply Bajakajian’s
standard against those “volumes of history.” U.S. Br. 18,
20. That is wrong twice over.
a.  The State cites no instance of its historical laws’ being used to forfeit anything as valuable as an airplane for
anything as minor as a six-pack. Meanwhile, all four of
the federal government’s examples of extreme forfeiture
actions (Br. 14-15) ended with the government’s dropping
the case and returning the ships. Kevin Arlyck, The
Founders’ Forfeiture, 119 Colum. L. Rev. 1449, 1493 &
n.259 (2019) ( Ship Mary ); Order on Petition of William
Provost (D.N.Y. 1792), Order on Petition of Elijah Pell
(D.N.Y. 1793), and The Alfred (D.N.Y. 1795), all microformed on M886, Roll 1, at 118-19, 128-29, 180-81, 189-90,
309-11, 314-16 (Nat’l Archives & Recs. Admin.). And not
because the owners were necessarily blameless: In Provost’s case, Secretary Hamilton forfeited the alcohol
($14.84) but released the ship ($2,000). As the government’s own source explains, Founding-era practice reflected “strong proportionality considerations” for in rem
forfeitures. Arlyck, supra, at 1495.
b.  Whatever the status of historical in rem forfeitures, moreover, analogies to them were understood to
carry no weight for forfeitures openly imposed as punishment. “[D]isguise the matter as we may,” wrote Joel
Prentiss Bishop, “if the intent which the owner of property carries in his bosom is the gist of the thing on which
the forfeiture turns, then the question is one of the criminal law, and the forfeiture is a penalty imposed for crime.”

8


1 Commentaries on the Criminal Law 395 (3d ed. 1865).
Criminal sentences “to forfeit particular articles of property,” he added, “rest on the same reasons as fines.” Id.
at 402. Rufus Waples agreed: Using in rem forfeiture as
“a disguised method of punishing for crime” would be unprecedented. A Treatise on Proceedings in Rem  28
(1882).
2.  Equally misplaced is the federal government’s view
that, because early Americans sometimes half-implied
that the guilty-property fiction masked “latent penal objectives,” historical in rem forfeitures bless modern criminal ones. U.S. Br. 17, 20. Again, Bajakajian says differently, relying on the very Justice Story quote the government surgically rearranges for the opposite proposition.
U.S. Br. 17. The government’s claim (Br. 17) that “the in
rem/in personam distinction makes no difference here”
cuts against it also: Because modern in rem and in personam forfeitures generally are “designed to punish the offender,” both are subject to the Excessive Fines Clause
“regardless of whether the proceeding is styled in rem or
in personam.” Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 331 n.6, 332; Austin, 509 U.S. at 621-22 (holding that the Clause applies to
in rem forfeitures that are at least partly punitive). Or
even take the government on its own terms. If everyone
quietly thought the guilty-property fiction was fraudulent, the answer would not be to extend  that fraud to undisputedly punitive forfeitures, but—in an appropriate
case—to revisit decisions resting on it.
C. The State’s instrumentality model invites confusion and abuse.
Practical considerations confirm the point. The State
would replace Bajakajian’s standard with a proportionality-free inquiry into “whether forfeited property ‘has a
close enough relationship to the offense’ to be an

9


instrumentality.” Resp. Br. 23. But what is “close
enough”? The State says “a building where ‘an isolated
drug sale happens to occur’” is not, Resp. Br. 39, yet an
airplane with a six-pack is. But why? The building facilitates the drug sale much as the plane facilitates the alcohol offense. Or must property be “indispensable” to the
crime? Resp. Br. 40. If so, that would be news to the jurisdictions that routinely forfeit property involved  in offenses but not indispensable to them. And it would exempt Jouppi’s plane here; goods reach Beaver by river
barge too.
For its part, the federal government suggests (Br. 13)
that Bajakajian’s standard rewards offenders who “use
a Lamborghini” instead of a “jalopy.” But that otherwiseidentical offenses can yield “dramatic variations in the
value of conveyances” forfeited is reason to question forfeiture statutes, not the Constitution’s checks on them.
Austin, 509 U.S. at 621. Nor is the Excessive Fines
Clause reserved for the Lamborghini set. For one thing,
the offense’s gravity is only half the proportionality inquiry; the other half is the magnitude of the fine. Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 334. And on that separate question—not at issue here (Cert. Reply 5)—several courts
consider “the owner’s economic means” “relative to the
property’s value.” State v. Timbs, 134 N.E.3d 12, 36 (Ind.
2019); Timbs v. Indiana, 586 U.S. 146, 152 (2019) (noting
open question). For another, the remedy need not be allor-nothing; in federal courts, for instance, forfeitures may
be “reduce[d]” rather than eliminated “as necessary to
avoid a violation of the Excessive Fines Clause.” 18 U.S.C.
§ 983(g)(4).
Meanwhile, the State’s proportionality-free standard
invites abuse; for civil and criminal forfeitures alike,
“[o]ne can easily imagine cases in which Justice Scalia’s

10


freestanding instrumentality approach could lead to results that would seem grossly unfair.” United States v. 25
Sandra Ct., 135 F.3d 462, 465-66 (7th Cir. 1998). In Bajakajian, the government conceded that the approach
might allow forfeiting “the Taj Mahal” if used to sell a
“teaspoon of marijuana.” Tr. at 13-14, United States v.
Bajakajian (No. 96-1487). In Timbs, Indiana conceded
that an only-just-speeding Bugatti would be a forfeitable
“instrumentality” of speeding. Tr. at 43-45, Timbs v. Indiana (No. 17-1091). Nor are those hypotheticals so farfetched. In 2015, for instance, the government seized a
new pickup for exporting “munitions of war”—in the form
of five lawfully owned bullets and a magazine, unwittingly
left in the console. Serrano v. CBP, 975 F.3d 488, 493 (5th
Cir. 2020). If the Court entertains the State’s instrumentality theory at all, it should be rejected.
II. On the question presented, the judgment below
should be reversed.
“If the amount of [a] forfeiture is grossly disproportional to the gravity of the defendant’s offense, it is unconstitutional.” Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 337. Our position—like most courts’—is that evaluating the gravity of
a defendant’s offense includes considering his specific actions, not taking a purely abstract view of the crime. The
standard below does the opposite.
A. A fine’s excessiveness is evaluated, not purely
in the abstract, but by reference to the gravity
of the defendant’s misconduct.
Text, precedent, history, and the Clause’s function
confirm that a fine’s excessiveness must be evaluated with
reference to the defendant’s own misconduct. Whoever
sets a fine, whatever purpose it serves, whatever form it
takes, the Clause measures it against “the gravity of the

11


defendant’s offense”—which requires evaluating what
the defendant did.
1.  The State concedes (Br. 27) that “[a]n Excessive
Fines Clause analysis requires an examination of a defendant’s culpability.” Yet it argues courts cannot undertake that analysis when fines are set by law. E.g., Resp.
Br. 33. Each permutation of this argument fails.
a.  The State’s main theme is that, given legislative
“primacy,” fines set by law deserve substantial deference.
Resp. Br. 32.3 That bears little on the question presented.
Whatever deference Bajakajian contemplated was built
into its interpreting “excessive,” not as requiring strict
proportionality, but as forbidding gross disproportionality. 524 U.S. at 336-37. The Court nowhere suggested that
the defendant’s specific actions were irrelevant to “the
gravity of [his] offense.” Id. at 337. Rather, the Court presupposed that “factual findings” inform the inquiry, id. at
336-37 n.10, then spent pages situating Bajakajian at the
low end of the statute’s spectrum of culpability, id. at 337-
40. Little wonder most courts read the standard as
“look[ing] at the overall circumstances, including seriousness of the offense and personal benefit or culpability.”
Yskamp v. DEA, 163 F.3d 767, 773 (3d Cir. 1998).
The State denies that Bajakajian stands for any such
thing. On the State’s telling, this Court invalidated Bajakajian’s forfeiture, not because his misconduct was minor, but because Congress didn’t truly mean to “target[]”
low-level offenders like him. Resp. Br. 42. Because
Alaska’s legislature really meant to target low-level

3 Elsewhere, the federal government has gone further, demanding
deference for fines calculated by the Executive Branch and not mandated by statute. See generally Appellant’s Br. at 51-54, United
States v. Saydam, No. 26-503 (9th Cir. May 15, 2026).

12


offenders, the State says, that ends the analysis. Resp.
Br. 34, 41-42.
That reading blinks reality. As here, Bajakajian’s offense of conviction covered relatively minor violations;
those committed “while violating another law of the
United States” carried double the maximum fine and
prison term under an adjoining sub-provision. Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 350 (Kennedy, J., dissenting) (citation omitted). Yet the forfeiture provision covered all, major and minor alike. 18 U.S.C. § 982(a)(1) (1988 & Supp. V
1993). As the Court recognized, Congress thus “did not
view the reporting offense” as “trivial,” even for Bajakajian. 524 U.S. at 339 n.14. Even so, while legislatures
certainly may set mandatory penalties, U.S. Br. 23, they
cannot override the Constitution’s guarantee that, in any
particular case, excessive fines shall not be imposed.
Nor is it clear how courts are meant to execute the
(decidedly undeferential) task the State envisions: reading statutes and divining what subset of textually covered
defendants lawmakers subjectively  wanted to “target[].”
Resp. Br. 41. Evidently, Bajakajian was not such a defendant. Yet even today, the federal government pursues
crippling fines for less serious reporting missteps—all
while insisting the Excessive Fines Clause poses no obstacle. E.g., Def.’s Opp. Mot. Summ. J. at 32-33, United
States v. Chen-Baker, No. 22-cv-256 (W.D.N.Y. Oct. 22,
2025) (Doc. 43-1) (challenging $108,000 in penalties for
non-willful reporting errors, corresponding to $25 in late
taxes). And of course, all this distracts from the most obvious point: Governments’ desire for excessive fines, even
if deeply felt, is precisely what the Clause exists to check.
b.  The State also errs in discounting history. For centuries, abusive economic sanctions have been inflated by
“mak[ing] faults where they are not” or “mak[ing] them

13


greater than in themselves they are.” Proceedings in the
Star-Chamber against Henry Sherfield  (1633), 3 T.B.
Howell, State Trials 519, 546 (1816). Against that backdrop, excessive-fines protections ensured that fines would
be imposed only “according to the degree of the fault.”
Jones v. Commonwealth, 5 Va. 555, 557 (1799) (Carrington, J.).
The State dismisses that history because fines often
were set by “individual officials,” not legislatures. Resp.
Br. 25 (emphasis omitted). But the Founding generation
well understood that excessive-fines protections would
check legislatures as well. See Harmelin v. Michigan, 501
U.S. 957, 975-76 (1991) (opinion of Scalia, J.); Timbs, 586
U.S. at 165-67 (Thomas, J., concurring in the judgment).
And by 1868, scores of abusive fines were enshrined in
legislation that even the State recoils at defending.
c.  The State further argues that considering the facts
of a defendant’s wrongdoing is unadministrable and “an
intrusion.” Resp. Br. 31 (citation omitted). But in other
contexts, judges perform that task every day. Pet. Br. 34.
Bajakajian likewise contemplated that, in applying the
Excessive Fines Clause, courts would analyze “the facts
of a particular case.” 524 U.S. at 336-37 n.10. And for decades, most courts have done so (Pet. 16-23), with no ill effects that the State has identified.
d.  Nor does it follow that because severe prison terms
have survived Cruel and Unusual Punishments challenges, “the same deference” applies to fines. Resp. Br.
33. The State observes (Br. 31) that Bajakajian drew its
standard from Cruel and Unusual Punishments precedents. 524 U.S. at 336. That analogy, however, explains
the Court’s “reject[ing] a ‘strict proportionality’ standard”; it did not require courts “to apply deference anew in
each case.” Robson 200, LLC v. City of Lakeland, 593 F.

14


Supp. 3d 1110, 1120 (M.D. Fla. 2022). Moreover, such an
approach would be uniquely ill-suited for the Excessive
Fines Clause. Pet. Br. 42-43.
More broadly, the State’s argument is non-responsive
to the question presented. The State calls prison-term
cases “instructive” but never says how, beyond insisting
that the Excessive Fines Clause sets a “high hurdle” for
relief. Resp. Br. 32. And perhaps it does; even courts on
petitioner’s side of the split describe prevailing defendants as “the unusual [ones] who c[an] overcome the high
hurdle of showing gross disproportionality.” State v.
Timbs, 169 N.E.3d 361, 376 (Ind. 2021). But that says
nothing about whether courts should evaluate the offense’s gravity purely in the abstract or with reference to
the defendant’s specific wrongdoing.
2.  The federal government admits that “individualized
circumstances of an offender’s conduct can be relevant”—
but not, it hastens to add, when an “objective[]” of forfeiture is to “depriv[e] him of the instruments of the offense.” U.S. Br. 8, 22. On that view, forfeiting property
(however valuable) for use in a crime (however minor) is
necessarily proportioned to the “incapacitative rationale”
of “preventing its use for further crimes.” U.S. Br. 30. If
that sounds like the government’s failed bid in Austin to
exempt forfeitures from the Excessive Fines Clause entirely, that’s because it is. U.S. Br. at 23, 32, Austin v.
United States, 509 U.S. 602 (1993) (No. 92-6073). Wrong
then, wrong now. The Clause forbids a forfeiture that incapacitates out of all proportion, just as it forbids one that
punishes out of all proportion. And whether a forfeiture
does so turns on what the defendant did. In real-world
terms, moreover, the government’s incapacitative rationale rings especially hollow; in one of the only other
publicly covered cases involving dry-village airplane

15


forfeitures, the State returned the plane to the defendant
after leveraging a $35,000 pay-out. Kyle Hopkins, Pilot
Pleads Guilty in Bootlegging Case , Anchorage Daily
News (June 13, 2008), https://tinyurl.com/4h3jwpzt.
The State also insists that not just “the harm caused,”
but also the harm “ threatened” factors into the analysis.
Resp. Br. 35 (citation omitted). No quarrel there; Bajakajian considered the potential for harm “had [Bajakajian’s] crime gone undetected.” 524 U.S. at 339. The
point is not that Jouppi’s offense was “harmless” (Resp.
Br. 43); in the main, the Excessive Fines Clause “ presume[s] that some crime was committed that caused
harm.” United States v. $11,500.00, 869 F.3d 1062, 1074
n.8 (9th Cir. 2017). But potential harm, like actual harm,
varies with the defendant’s wrongdoing—except under
the decision below. Pet. App. 25a n.94.
The State’s drunk-driving analogy (Br. 36) illustrates
the point. Most drunk-driving offenses risk grave harm.
(Though in Alaska, drunk drivers, like drunk pilots, face
mandatory forfeiture only upon a third conviction. Alaska
Stat. §§ 28.35.030(b)(3), (n)(5).) But here, too, culpability
and risk can vary—say, a tipsy patron who sleeps it off in
his back seat in a State where that counts as a DUI. See
United States v. McFarland , 369 F. Supp. 2d 54, 58-59
(D. Me. 2005). Even the State’s chief drunk-driving case
applied nothing like the standard below. State v. O’Malley, 206 N.E.3d 662, 686 (Ohio 2022).
3.  The federal government dwells on the form of the
fine, observing (Br. 28-29) that many historical abuses involved monetary fines, not forfeitures. But as the Court
has explained—in a case involving property used in criminal activity— “in personam  criminal forfeiture .  . . is
clearly a form of monetary punishment no different, for
Eighth Amendment purposes, from a traditional ‘fine.’”

16


Alexander, 509 U.S. at 558. Moreover, the government
pressed the same cash/in-kind distinctions in Austin.
E.g., U.S. Br., Austin, supra, at 15, 26. As Justice Scalia
pinpointed then, however, “for the Eighth Amendment to
limit cash fines while permitting limitless in-kind assessments would make little sense, altering only the form of
the Star Chamber abuses.” Austin, 509 U.S. at 624 (opinion concurring in part and concurring in the judgment).
Now, the government outright embraces that result: A
“$95,000 monetary fine” might be excessive, but forfeiting
Jouppi’s airplane (whatever its value) is not. U.S. Br. 30.
The State notes that some dangers of civil forfeiture
are absent from criminal forfeiture. Resp. Br. 29, 40-41.
But others are very much present, including grossly disproportional fines. Worse, every principle the State urges
would apply equally to the civil forfeitures it disclaims. As
for its assurance (Br. 5) that civil forfeitures are rare in
Alaska, that (a) is unfalsifiable, given Alaska’s distinction
as one of the three worst States for forfeiture transparency; and (b) ignores the civil forfeitures routed through
federal agencies, which channel millions of dollars in revenue back to Alaska law enforcement. Inst. for Just., Policing for Profit: The Abuse of Civil Asset Forfeiture 54,
82 (4th ed. 2026). Regardless, the standard here will apply
nationwide.
B. The Alaska Supreme Court’s judgment should
be reversed.
The decision below evaluated the gravity of Ken
Jouppi’s offense purely in the abstract—in terms equally
applicable to every potential violator of the statute. That
cannot be squared with the Excessive Fines Clause.
1.  To start, the State says (Br. 2) that the question
presented “fights a strawman” because the court below
analyzed Jouppi’s “actual circumstances.” Presumably,

17


this Court “‘necessarily considered and rejected’” that
contention “in granting certiorari.” Stolt-Nielsen S.A. v.
AnimalFeeds Int’l Corp. , 559 U.S. 662, 670 n.2 (2010);
Cert. Reply 2. It is equally misplaced now. Every consideration the Alaska Supreme Court cited applies equally
to Jouppi and to every violator of the statute. Every  convicted defendant is “within the class of persons targeted
by the statute.” Pet. App. 20a. On the court’s six-pack
premise, every  violation has “the potential to cause the
exact harm targeted by the law.” Resp. Br. 43; Pet. App.
24a. A standard that cashes out identically for every offender is one that evaluates the offense “purely in the abstract.” Pet. i.
2.  The State’s defense of the judgment below confirms
the methodological error.
a.  The State stresses that alcohol abuse is a real problem in Alaska. Undisputed. Pet. Br. 41. The question is
whether it matters to the excessive-fines analysis if an offender is Al Capone or Ken Jouppi. The State and the decision below say no. That is the error meriting reversal.
Shot through the State’s brief (e.g., at 44-45) is the related assumption that violations of this particular statute
are so categorically serious that the degree of a defendant’s wrongdoing cannot possibly matter. Of course, the
statute belies that assumption—not least because it classifies Jouppi’s variant as a misdemeanor. More to the
point, that assumption is  the error below, repackaged.
Under the decision below, once a State shows that the legislature “reasonably” thought a statute addressed a serious problem (Resp. Br. 39), the defendant’s particular
wrongdoing is irrelevant. Consider the State’s own example. Obviously “[a] marijuana trafficker cannot challenge
his conviction on the grounds that marijuana is harmless.”
Resp. Br. 46. But in terms of the gravity of the offense, a

18


grandma with a gummy in her nightstand is not remotely
comparable to the trafficker.
Except that, under the standard below, she is. Why
not forfeit her home for the gummy? Or a car for “the remains of a marijuana cigarette in the ashtray”? United
States v. 1986 Mercedes Benz, 846 F.2d 2, 4 (2d Cir. 1988).
Why not forfeit  the pickup for a forgotten bullet at the
border? Just as the federal government theorizes (Br. 27)
that a six-pack might “whet[] a recovering alcoholic’s
taste for liquor,” a gunman could steal the bullet and fire
the shot that sparks a cartel war. For that matter, why
not forfeit the family minivan because Dad packs one of
his prescription Ambien for Mom? Or their home, if he
hands her the pill indoors? Each involves a felony: distributing a Schedule IV drug—and amid a prescription-drugabuse epidemic. How do any of those cases differ from
this one? And if they don’t (and, plainly, they don’t), how
can the standard below square with text, precedent, history, and the Excessive Fines Clause’s basic function?
Or take low-level speeding and seatbelt violations,
which likewise carry “the potential to cause the exact
harm targeted by the law.” Resp. Br. 43. Why wouldn’t
exorbitant fines and forfeitures for those  offenses pass
muster below? The State offers only that such punishments might not be “rational.” Resp. Br. 43 (citation omitted). But setting aside that rational-basis review is not for
fundamental rights, why  wouldn’t  they be rational?
Above fifteen miles per hour, “small changes in speed
yield relatively large increases in risk” of pedestrian injury and death. Brian C. Tefft, Impact Speed and a Pedestrian’s Risk of Severe Injury or Death, AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety 12 (2011). So why  couldn’t cashstrapped cities do just what Justice Breyer hypothesized
in Timbs? And why be sure one never would? Vehicles are

19


a tempting source of revenue. And it’s hardly unheard-of
for senior officials to pressure prosecutors to “increase
forfeiture income” to hit “budget target[s].” Mem. from
William P. Barr, Acting Deputy Att’y Gen., to all U.S. Attorneys (July 18, 1990), https://tinyurl.com/56rt9t4k.
At base, the State submits that “Alaska is different.”
Sturgeon v. Frost, 577 U.S. 424, 438 (2016). In many ways
it is; its independent streak drew Ken Jouppi there five
decades ago. But not in its relation to the Constitution,
whose incorporated protections have “the same meaning
in all parts of the United States.” Wolford v. Lopez, 609
U.S. 185, 206 (2026). And under the standard below, it is
hard to imagine any fine anywhere that would be excessive. Conspicuously, the State itself identifies none—besides Hosep Bajakajian’s and the literal Black Codes. But
cf. State v. Manuel, 20 N.C. 144, 161-63 (1838) (rejecting
state-law excessive-fines challenge to early Black Code,
using reasoning much like Alaska’s).
b.  The State’s remaining arguments reduce to one
theme: carte blanche.
The State claims (Br. 43) that “ mens rea acts as a
guardrail” against excessive fines. That is no truer here
than in Bajakajian. There, the forfeiture involved a specific-intent felony. See 524 U.S. at 325. Here, the State
maintains that Jouppi’s misdemeanor can rest merely on
his not performing dragnet searches—even with “no actual knowledge of any alcohol” in passengers’ luggage.
State’s Alaska Sup. Ct. Br. 27. Simply, the scienter for a
misdemeanor says little about whether a $95,000 forfeiture is excessive.
The Alaska Supreme Court’s reliance on maximum
fines is of a piece. The State notes (Br. 16, 46) that
Jouppi’s plane was worth “only” 9.5 times the $10,000
maximum fine. But Bajakajian’s forfeiture ($357,000) was

20


just 1.4 times his maximum fine ($250,000), never mind
the five-year maximum prison term. Pet. Br. 40-41. That
ratio did not scuttle his claim for an obvious reason: “The
statutory maximum” is “designed as an outer limit on the
punishment available” and “does not necessarily reflect
an individual offender’s culpability or the gravity of the
actual offense giving rise to forfeiture.” von Hofe v.
United States , 492 F.3d 175, 187 (2d Cir. 2007). Hence
why Bajakajian looked to the individualized Guidelines
range, not a one-size-fits-all maximum. Pet. Br. 40.
Consistent with the rest of its standard, moreover, the
Alaska Supreme Court’s focus on maximum theoretical
fines leaves it to legislatures to decide “what a fine should
be and whether it’s excessive.” Yates v. Pinellas Hematology & Oncology, P.A. , 21 F.4th 1288, 1318 (11th Cir.
2021) (Newsom, J., concurring). Today, for instance,
Alaska’s maximum misdemeanor fine is not $10,000, but
$25,000. Input that variable into the standard below (9.5
× $25,000) and a $237,500 airplane could be forfeited.
Meanwhile, the corporate maximum is $500,000. So had
KenAir LLC owned the plane—rather than Ken Jouppi,
human—the standard below would reflexively bless forfeiting a $4,750,000 aircraft over the same six-pack.
c.  Finally, the State tars Jouppi. Having acknowledged that the decision below took as its premise that “his
culpability extended only to one six-pack and that he had
no related misconduct” (Br. in Opp. 14), the State now declares that “Jouppi’s crime was not flying in ‘a six-pack’”
and insinuates recidivism. Resp. Br. 1 (emphasis added),
47 n.6. But see Cert. Reply 10. Having conceded below
that “jurors could have found that Jouppi had actual
knowledge of the six-pack and no willful blindness as to
the remaining alcohol” (State’s Alaska Sup. Ct. Br. 28), it
now dwells on that other alcohol. Resp. Br. 1, 44. Having

21


waived the chance to present evidence of related misconduct at the excessive-fines hearing—despite the trial
court’s invitation (Tr. Vol. II 192-95 (4/19/2018 Hrg.))—it
now claims it tried to do just that. Resp. Br. 15. But see
Cert. Reply 9.
Even the State, it seems, thinks facts should matter
more than they do under the decision below. On that much
we agree. And it is not “glib” to describe that decision accurately: an airplane for a six-pack. Nor is this a laughing
matter for Ken Jouppi. No less than the State, he appreciates the importance of dry-village laws. R. p. 678; Pet.
Br. 5. Yet for years, the State put him in an impossible
bind. On pain of “willful blindness” accusations, it left
him—an aging bush pilot—to play detective: to confront
and search suspected criminals on isolated airstrips, with
neither the authority nor the protections of law enforcement. When he did identify bootleggers, authorities were
as likely as not to treat him as a nuisance. R. pp. 677-78.
Adding injury to insult, the State has now spent fourteenand-a-half years gunning for his airplane. And under the
Alaska Supreme Court’s standard, any jurisdiction can do
the same and worse for violating virtually any law on the
books. The Excessive Fines Clause demands more: It
asks not what the worst violator of a statute might deserve, but what Jouppi actually did—“the real measure of
his own offence.” Jones, 5 Va. at 558 (Carrington, J.).

22


CONCLUSION
The judgment below should be reversed and the case
remanded for further proceedings.
